opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For me, the excitement comes from a question social scientists have wrestled with for a very long time: how do we study a system as complex as human society when we can't really run experiments on it? You can't rerun history. You can't just change a policy for a whole city and see what happens without real consequences for real people. So much of what we know comes from observing after the fact, or from small, controlled lab studies that don't always generalize to the messiness of the real world.

Simulation has always held out a promise here. Going back decades, people built agent-based models, little worlds where individual agents follow rules and you watch collective behavior emerge. Schelling's segregation model is the classic example. Those were powerful ideas, but the agents were quite thin. They followed a handful of hand-written rules, and human behavior is so much richer than that. People have memories, relationships, goals, they reflect on what's happened to them, they talk to each other and change their minds.

What's different now is that large language models give us a way to build agents that capture a lot more of that richness. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human experience through text, so when you put them in the right architecture, with memory, reflection, and planning, you start to get behavior that feels believably human. That was the motivation behind our work on generative agents, where we put twenty-five agents in a little town and watched things like information spread, relationships form, and a party come together without us scripting any of it.

The reason that matters is that it opens up the possibility of a kind of laboratory for society. Imagine being able to test how a community might react to a new policy, how misinformation might travel through a network, or how a design decision on a social platform might shape the way people interact, before you deploy it to millions of real people. Moving from a world where we only learn from consequences to one where we can explore possible futures first is a real shift.

I want to be careful, too. These simulations are only useful if they're grounded and validated, if we can show the agents reflect how real people and real groups behave, including the diversity and the disagreements. That's a big part of the work ahead. But the opportunity is that, for the first time, the tools may finally be rich enough to match the ambition social scientists have had for a long time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that for most of the history of the social sciences, we've been studying human behavior with instruments that are really blunt. If you want to understand how people might respond to a new policy, or how misinformation spreads through a community, or what happens when you change the rules of a market, your options have basically been surveys, lab experiments with a few hundred undergrads, or looking back at historical data and hoping the past tells you something about the future. All of those are valuable, but they're slow, they're expensive, and a lot of the most important questions you simply can't run as an experiment because it would be unethical or impossible.

Simulation has always been the dream answer to that. The idea of agent-based modeling goes back decades: build a little world, populate it with agents that follow some rules, and watch what emerges. The problem was that the agents were cartoons. You'd give them three or four if-then rules, and the behavior you got out was only as rich as the rules you put in. You couldn't ask them an open-ended question. They didn't remember anything. They didn't have anything resembling a personality or a history.

What changed is that large language models give us, for the first time, agents that can behave in ways that are plausibly human across a very wide range of situations. They can hold a conversation, reflect on what happened to them, form a plan, change their mind. So suddenly the simulation isn't a cartoon anymore. When we built Smallville, the little town of twenty-five generative agents, what struck me wasn't any single behavior but that things like a Valentine's Day party happened because one agent decided to throw it, told a few friends, and the information propagated socially. Nobody scripted that.

So the excitement, for me, is that we might be able to build a kind of wind tunnel for social science. Before you build a bridge, you test a model of it. We've never really had that for policies or for products or for interventions in communities. If we can make simulated people that are faithful enough to real people, and I want to stress that fidelity is the hard, unsolved part, then a researcher or a policymaker could ask "what if" questions and get a meaningful answer before touching the real world.

And the second piece I find exciting is almost the reverse direction. Building these simulations forces you to be explicit about your theory of human behavior. When the simulation gets something wrong, that's data too. It tells you where your understanding of people breaks down. So it's not just a tool for prediction. It's a new way of doing the science itself.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is the possibility of studying how individual behavior gives rise to collective outcomes. We make choices, interact with other people, and respond to our environment. Out of those interactions emerge things like norms, institutions, and social movements. But that connection between the individual and the collective is very difficult to study directly.

Simulation gives us a way to ask “what if?” What if we changed a policy, or the way people communicate? Could we explore the consequences before making a change in the real world, where experiments can be expensive or sometimes unethical?

The opportunity with language models is that we may be able to represent a richer range of human behavior than we could with simple, hand-written rules. That doesn’t mean a simulated society automatically tells us how a real society works. We have to validate these models and understand where they fail. But if we can do that, simulation could become a useful complement to experiments and observation—a way to develop hypotheses and explore social possibilities that would otherwise be hard to examine.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me about simulation is the possibility of connecting individual behavior to patterns that emerge at the level of a community. Each of us has a limited perspective, but our interactions produce institutions, social norms, and collective outcomes that can be difficult to understand by looking at one person at a time.

Simulation gives us a way to explore that connection. If we build agents that can represent meaningful aspects of human behavior, we can ask: What happens when we change the environment? What happens when information travels differently, or when we introduce a different policy? And we can examine how those changes play out through many interactions.

The important qualification is that a simulation is only useful to the extent that we can validate it. A world that looks believable isn’t necessarily an accurate model of society. But if we can establish where these models capture human behavior and where they fail, they could become a powerful tool for developing hypotheses and exploring possible consequences before making changes in the real world.
